dialogue.literal_gloss: Kunyangwe [to / at nyangwe] • zvainetsa [zvainetsa] • akakwanisa [he/she (past) kwanisa] • kupedza [to / at pedza] • chikoro [school]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akakwanisa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akakwanisa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('zvainetsa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'zvainetsa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

cultural_notes.title: Perseverance in Education ('Kupedza Chikoro') Against the Odds
cultural_notes.content: Completing one's education ('kupedza chikoro') despite financial or practical hardships ('kunyangwe zvainetsa') is deeply admired across Zimbabwe, where families make immense sacrifices to see their children graduate.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new family sentence into English: 'Hanzvadzi yangu inoshanda muguta reHarare.'
options: My parents live at the rural homestead in Masvingo.
My sibling works in the city of Harare.
My friend passed all her school examinations this year.
The baby is sleeping quietly inside the bedroom.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Hanzvadzi yangu' = 'My sibling (brother/sister)', 'inoshanda' = 'works', 'muguta reHarare' = 'in the city of Harare'.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence using the Present Progressive ('is reading right now'): 'Shamwari yangu ______ bhuku idzva.'
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shamwari' uses the progressive form 'iri ku-' + '-verenga' (read) to mean 'is reading right now'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Ndeipi shangu yaunoda, nhema kana tsvuku?'
options: Where did you put my white shirt and blue trousers?
These new shoes are very comfortable for walking.
She washed all the white clothes this morning.
Which shoe do you want, the black one or the red one?
active_exercises.correct_answer: Which shoe do you want, the black one or the red one?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Ndeipi shangu yaunoda' = 'Which shoe do you want', 'nhema kana tsvuku' = 'the black one or the red one'.
